extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining whether claim language is definite under 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA §112, second paragraph) including treatment of relative/subjective terms, numerical ranges, functional language, antecedent basis, references to other claims, and Markush/alternative groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of degree / relative terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the specification uses the same term of degree as in the claim, a rejection is proper if the scope of the term is not understood when read in light of the specification; when relative terms are used where the improvement rests entirely upon size or weight of an element, the adequacy of disclosure of a standard is of greater criticality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the specification supplies an objective standard for the degree/relative term; rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) are proper when scope is unclear. Example cases: In re Wiggins. If the term's boundaries are not discernible, require amendment or further disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to a variable object
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be indefinite by reference to an object that is variable (e.g., reciting relationships to an unspecified user or rider of unspecified build).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claim specifies the positional/measurement relationship or a known standard. Examples: Ex parte Miyazaki (printer/user height indefinite), Ex parte Brummer (bicycle rider of unspecified build indefinite), Orthokinetics (pediatric wheelchair 'so dimensioned' held definite because as accurate as subject matter permits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'about' (approximations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The range encompassed by the term 'about' depends on the context of the specification and claims; 'about' can be definite if the limitation can be clearly assessed (e.g., measurable via stopwatch) but may be indefinite where there is close prior art and no indication of range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider specification context, prosecution history, prior art, and whether a POSITA can determine the covered range. Example: Ortho-McNeil Pharm. v. Caraco; W.L. Gore (stretch rate 'exceeding about 10% per second' definite), Amgen (problems with 'at least about' where no guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'essentially'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'essentially' can be definite when the specification provides guidelines and examples sufficient to enable a POSITA to draw a line between unavoidable impurities and essential ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specification gives general guidelines or examples that delineate the boundary (e.g., In re Marosi holding 'essentially free of alkali metal' definite). Do not require arbitrary numeric cutoffs if purpose and guidance are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'similar' (vague comparative terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'similar' in claim recitations are indefinite if it is unclear what apparatus or structure the applicant intended to cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the specification to see if 'similar' is defined or exemplified; absent that, find the claim indefinite. Examples: Ex parte Kristensen (no clarity for 'similar apparatus'), Ex parte Pappas (design claim 'similar structure' indefinite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'substantially' (terms of breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Substantially' is a broad term; it can be definite if the specification contains general guidelines allowing a POSITA to know what is meant, or indefinite if it lacks boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate specification examples/guidelines and prior art; examples include In re Nehrenberg, In re Mattison, Andrew Corp. v. Gabriel Electronics. If the spec provides general criteria, 'substantially' may be acceptable; otherwise, consider rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of 'type' to an expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding 'type' (e.g., 'ZSM-5-type') can extend scope and render a claim indefinite if it is unclear what 'type' conveys, especially when dependent claims fall outside the asserted genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether 'type' is defined or supported; examples: Ex parte Copenhaver, Ex parte Attig. If unclear, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Facially subjective claim language (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing', 'unobtrusive manner', 'comparable', 'superior') may render claims indefinite where the specification supplies no objective standard for measuring the scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require an objective standard in the specification or evidence that a POSITA can ascertain the meaning; applicant may amend to remove the subjective term or provide evidence/definitions. Cases: Datamize (aesthetically pleasing indefinite), Interval Licensing (unobtrusive manner indefinite), Ex parte Anderson. Note: some subjective terms may still be definite if the spec supplies sufficiently clear boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical ranges and amounts — general
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of specific numerical ranges generally does not raise definiteness issues, but context matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether ranges create unclear metes and bounds; if boundaries are discernible, ranges are acceptable. See detailed subrules for narrower-in-broader, open-ended ranges, and effective amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow and broader ranges in the same claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim that includes both a broad range and a narrower range may be indefinite when the claim's boundaries are not discernible (e.g., 'between 45 and 78°C, preferably between 50 and 60°C').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer placing examples/preferences in the specification or in dependent/other independent claims. If it's unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation, make a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Dependent claims reciting narrower ranges are acceptable (e.g., claim 1: 70-150 ohms; claim 2: 70-100 ohms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended numerical ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended ranges (e.g., 'at least 20%') must be carefully analyzed for definiteness, particularly with dependent claims that could create apparent contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether dependent claim recitations create ambiguities (e.g., nonsodium ingredients summing to 100% seeming to exclude 'at least' sodium). Note that theoretically impossible compositions in claim language are not necessarily indefinite (subject matter that cannot exist cannot anticipate or infringe). See In re Kroekel, In re Kirsch, In re Mochel.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Effective amount' phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'an effective amount' may be definite if a POSITA could determine specific values from the disclosure; it may be indefinite if the function to be achieved is not stated or multiple effects are implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specification and examples teach what an effective amount is for the stated function. Examples: In re Mattison (test), In re Halleck (definite where not critical), In re Fredericksen (indefinite when function not stated). Applicant may clarify by stating function or giving examples/guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary claim language ('for example,' 'such as')
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing examples or preferences belongs properly in the specification rather than the claims; using phrases like 'for example' or 'such as' in claims may lead to confusion about scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' does not by itself render a claim indefinite, but examine factually. Examples of problematic phrasing include 'R is halogen, for example, chlorine' and 'material such as rock wool or asbestos.' Apply MPEP § 2173.02 guidance when making 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear due to missing antecedent basis (e.g., referring to 'said lever' when no earlier recitation of a lever exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that antecedent problems are typically correctable drafting oversights; examiners should identify and suggest corrections in a constructive manner. However, failure to provide an antecedent basis can render a claim indefinite (In re Packard). The absence of explicit antecedent wording does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable (Ex parte Porter, Bose Corp.). Also, omission of elements from a preamble does not per se make a claim indefinite if the claim body apprises a POSITA of scope (In re Larsen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to limitations in another claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Referring to a preceding claim to define a limitation (e.g., 'the product produced by the method of claim 1') is an acceptable claim construction and not necessarily indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such references are acceptable unless the reference format causes confusion. Examine dependent claims for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d)/pre-AIA §112 fourth paragraph. See Ex parte Porter and MPEP guidance. If reference causes confusion, a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection may be proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is; functional language is not per se improper, and 35 U.S.C. 112(f) expressly authorizes means/step-plus-function claiming, but purely functional limitations that provide no structure may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate functional limitations in context (specification disclosure and POSITA knowledge). Consider whether the limitation (1) provides a clear indication of scope, (2) sets well-defined boundaries or only states a problem/result, and (3) would allow a POSITA to know what structure or steps are encompassed. Permit functional language when structure or examples are present (In re Schreiber, In re Barr, In re Venezia). Beware of claims that merely recite a problem/result or encompass all means to achieve a result (Ariad, Hyatt, Datamize). Applicant remedies include adding quantitative metrics, providing formulas and examples, supplying general guidelines, or amending to recite structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative limitations / Markush groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting a list of alternatives (Markush group) are generally acceptable when formatted as a closed group ('consisting of'), but an open list ('comprising'/'consisting essentially of') may be indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP § 706.03(y), § 2117, and § 803.02 for Markush treatment. If the claim intends to encompass combinations or mixtures, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member' or 'or mixtures thereof'). Breadth by itself is not indefiniteness (In re Gardner), but overly expansive groups that prevent POSITA from discerning metes and bounds may be indefinite. Consider election and restriction issues per Markush practice.
